newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Violence mars Sri Lanka's local election.
newsitem.headline: Violence mars Sri Lanka's local election.

text.p: A bomb blast rocked a village and fighting broke out between political rivals in many parts of Sri Lanka as voting for local councils opened on Friday.

The ruling People's Alliance (PA) coalition and the main opposition United National Party (UNP) were among 12 parties and 132 independent groups contesting the election, seen as the first political test for President Chandrika Kumaratunga and her government.

At least 10 people were wounded, four seriously, when a bomb exploded near a polling station in Koswatte village in the northcentral Puttalam district, 50 km (30 miles) from Colombo, the police elections secretariat said.
"A People's Alliance candidate has complained, accusing United National Party supporters of having thrown the bomb," an official at the secretariat told Reuters.

Police said about 70 incidents of violence had been reported since late on Thursday, most of them clashes between UNP and PA polling agents, who are allowed to stay outside voting centres to ensure free and fair polls.
Police in the central hill district of Kandy said they raided a small printing press and seized more than 1,000 counterfeit ballot papers late on Thursday.
But Colombo and its suburbs, which have been centres of violence during previous elections, were largely peaceful and saw brisk voting, election workers said.
"Colombo is very peaceful. There seems to be a feeling of mutual goodwill (among voters) towards each other," said government minister A.H.M. Fowzie, who is the PA's campaign coordinator for Colombo.

"We are counting on a high voter turnout," said opposition leader and former prime minister Ranil Wickremesinghe after casting his vote in Colombo. "If it is a free and fair election, the UNP will win."
The UNP said earlier this week it was concerned that a lot of violence during the campaign would keep voters away.

Police were out in force and speculation was rife that the government would impose a curfew soon after polling ended at 4 p.m. (1000 GMT). Police officers refused to comment on the possibility of a curfew.
Campaign violence started with the killing in February of a young coalition legislator in the southern town of Ratnapura.

The Centre for Monitoring Election Violence, an independent group, said there were 1,914 incidents of poll-related violence reported as of Thursday, making this the most violent local government election of recent years.
Some 10 million Sri Lankans are eligible to vote to elect 3,567 representatives to 238 local bodies.

The Elections Office says more than 100,000 public servants manned 8,246 polling stations across the island, except in the northern and eastern provinces where government troops are fighting Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam Tamil (LTTE) rebels.
